Inside eRPC

A source-code field guide for software engineers — features, architecture, and the Go modules that implement them

Compiled 2026-09-16 from the erpc/erpc repository and docs.erpc.cloud deep dives.

1. What eRPC is

eRPC is a fault-tolerant JSON-RPC proxy for EVM and SVM (Solana) chains, written in Go. A client sends an ordinary eth_getBlockByNumber or getBlock call to one URL; eRPC authenticates it, checks a finality-aware cache, orders candidate upstreams by live health, wraps the call in nested failsafe policies — timeout, retry, hedge, and optionally consensus — and races it across one or more provider endpoints, returning a byte-perfect answer with X-ERPC-* headers that explain every decision. The design premise, repeated throughout the codebase, is that the unknown-input fallthrough is the primary path: chains, vendors, methods, and error shapes are open-ended sets, so nothing load-bearing may depend on enumerating them.

Conceptually the system splits into two halves. The front half is protocol machinery that does not know what a block is: HTTP ingress and batching (erpc/http_server.go), authentication (auth/), project tenancy and rate-limit budgets (erpc/projects.go), the network layer with its in-flight multiplexer, cache, and selection policy (erpc/networks.go), and the failsafe executor that composes retry/hedge/timeout/consensus (erpc/network_executor.go, failsafe/). The back half is chain knowledge, isolated behind one interface: architecture/evm/ translates tags, splits ranges, and classifies finality; architecture/svm/ does the same for Solana; upstream/ speaks to individual endpoints with per-upstream budgets and circuit breakers; health/ measures everything; and data/ persists cache entries through pluggable connectors.

Orientation on the repository layout, top to bottom:

DirectoryWhat lives there

upstream/Upstream.Forward: block-availability gate, per-upstream budget permit, circuit breaker, client send, health recording. Also the rate limiter budget/autotuner and composite error extractor.
consensus/Multi-upstream agreement: executor.go participant slots, analysis.go canonical hashing and dedupe, rules.go short-circuit and dispute rules.
health/Per-upstream rolling health windows (10 × 6s buckets), DDSketch quantiles, block-head lag state.
internal/policy/The selection-policy engine: per-slot goroutines evaluating an embedded JavaScript policy on a sobek runtime and atomically publishing the upstream order.
data/Cache connectors (memory, Redis, PostgreSQL, DynamoDB, ScyllaDB, gRPC/BDS), cache policies, cache executors with their own failsafes.
auth/Strategy chain (secret, database, jwt, siwe, network), JWKS fetching, authorizer rate permits.

thirdparty/Vendor integrations (25+ files): each vendor's GetVendorSpecificErrorIfAny hook, chain-ID tables, credit-unit pricing.
failsafe/Standalone policy primitives: backoff computation, hedged execution, ring-buffer circuit breaker.

Everything after this chapter walks one subsystem per chapter, in roughly the order a request meets them: the pipeline (ch. 2), the multiplexer (ch. 3), tracing (ch. 4), finality and caching (ch. 5), block availability (ch. 6), failsafes (ch. 7), consensus (ch. 8), health and selection (ch. 9), EVM translation (ch. 10), errors (ch. 11), metrics (ch. 12), the SVM architecture (ch. 13), then the complete configuration reference (ch. 14), directives and headers (ch. 15), a glossary (ch. 16), and a suggested source-reading order (ch. 17).

2. The request pipeline

A JSON-RPC request enters eRPC as an HTTP POST to /{project}/{architecture}/{chain} — for example /main/evm/1 — or /{project}/{alias} such as /main/arbitrum. In erpc/http_server.go, createRequestHandler opens the root span Http.ReceivedRequest, gzipped bodies are handled at roughly line 374, Http.ReadBody (:396) and Http.ParseRequests (:420) follow, and a batch body is fanned out as one goroutine per JSON-RPC element at ~:465, with responses reassembled in original element order by erpc/http_batch_resp.go. parseUrlPath (:877) resolves the project/network identity; any non-POST/non-OPTIONS request is treated as a healthcheck.

Authentication runs next as a strategy chain in auth/registry.go (AuthRegistry.Authenticate, :46) and auth/authorizer.go (per-strategy rate permit, :117): secret, database, jwt, siwe, network — first success wins. Auth deliberately emits no spans. The project layer (erpc/projects.go, Project.Forward :130, AuthenticateConsumer :123, AcquireRateLimitPermit :374) takes the project-level rate-limit budget permit and runs architecture pre-forward hooks before handing off to the network.

Inside erpc/networks.go, Network.Forward (:1743) runs the network stage: tryServeStaticResponse (:1789) answers configured canned replies; the in-flight multiplexer deduplicates identical concurrent calls; cacheDal.Get (:1825) consults the finality-aware cache; PolicyEngine.GetOrderedInLane (:1863) reads the published upstream order; tryShortCircuitFutureBlock (definition :853) can answer a beyond-head block with a synthesized null without spending a rate-limit permit; the network rate permit is taken at :2022; and the request is prepared at prepareRequest (:2030, definition :2542).

The failsafe executor, networkExecutor.Run in erpc/network_executor.go (:164), composes the policy nesting and hands individual attempts to the upstream layer. Upstream.Forward in upstream/upstream.go (:543) applies shouldSkip (:578), takes the per-upstream budget permit (:591), sends via Client.SendRequest (:778), records health only for reverts (:911) and successful non-empty responses (:945), and runs upstream-scope failsafes (:964). On the way out, normalizeResponse (networks.go :3326) restores the caller's JSON-RPC id byte-for-byte, HttpServer.WriteResponse (:744) and setResponseHeaders (:1172) stamp X-ERPC-* diagnostics, and the cache write fires asynchronously.

Inside Network.Forward the order is: static responses → multiplexer (in-flight dedup by request hash, leader/follower) → cache read → selection-policy ordering → failsafe executor → upstream sweep.

StageSourceKey behavior
1 · HTTP ingresserpc/http_server.goparseUrlPath, batch goroutine fan-out, gzip, CORS, domain aliasing.
2 · Authauth/registry.goStrategy chain in order: secret, database, jwt, siwe, network; first success wins.
3 · Projecterpc/projects.gorateLimitBudget permit, HandleProjectPreForward hook, shadow fan-out after response.
4 · Networkerpc/networks.goStatic responses → multiplexer → cacheDal.Get → policyEngine.GetOrdered* → pre-forward hooks → future-block short-circuit.
5 · Failsafe executorerpc/network_executor.gotimeout(consensus?(retry(hedge(upstream)))); matched by method, finality, request kind.

Scope rules worth remembering early: the circuit breaker is upstream-scope only (validation rejects it at network scope), consensus is network-scope only (rejected at upstream scope), and cache connectors take their own failsafeForGets/failsafeForSets policies.

Edge cases. 1. Gzip laziness: JSON-RPC responses arrive as many small writes, so the gzip decision — and thus WriteHeader/Content-Encoding — is deferred until enough bytes exist (conditionalGzipWriter, http_server.go:2076; issue #990). 2. Batch bodies split at [ and process concurrently, but responses must reassemble in original element order. 3. Hedge legs returning empty don't win — a fast null from a lagging upstream does not end the race (except methods in retry.emptyResultAccept). 4. useUpstream bypasses the selection policy, which is why client-set directives are gated by allowClientDirectives.

3. Request lifecycle & the multiplexer

eRPC executes concurrent requests inside Network.Forward, and its central deduplication mechanism is the in-flight multiplexer: an identity-keyed sync.Map (inFlightRequests, networks.go:39) on each Network. The first request for a key becomes the leader and runs the full pipeline — cache read, selection policy, failsafe executor timeout(retry(hedge())), upstream round trip. Later identical requests become followers, consuming zero upstream quota and blocking on the leader's mlx.done channel. The core registration is a LoadOrStore race in Network.handleMultiplexing (:3050, store at :3066):

// Try to atomically register as the leader or become a follower.
// Loop handles the edge case where we find a closed multiplexer during cleanup.
for {
	mlx := NewMultiplexer(mlxHash)
	vinf, loaded := n.inFlightRequests.LoadOrStore(mlxHash, mlx)

	if !loaded {
		// Our multiplexer was stored, we're the leader
		return mlx, nil, nil
	}

	// Another request is already in flight - try to be a follower
	inf := vinf.(*Multiplexer)

	// Try to register as follower under lock to prevent race with cleanup's Wait()
	inf.mu.Lock()
	if inf.closed {
		// Leader already finished and cleanup started, can't be a follower.
		// Retry LoadOrStore - the old entry should be deleted soon, allowing
		// us to properly become the new leader (with our mlx stored in the map).
		inf.mu.Unlock()
		continue
	}

	inf.copyWg.Add(1)
	inf.mu.Unlock()

— erpc/networks.go:3062–3087 (verbatim, trimmed).

Three first principles fall out of this design. First: caller latency is decoupled from bookkeeping. Cache writes, shadow requests, metrics, and head polls all happen in background goroutines bounded by existing budgets; the response path only does what the response needs. The async cache write runs on a detached 10-second appCtx (networks.go:2426–2457) with the response held alive via AddRef()/DoneRef() reference counting, so a client disconnect never aborts it. Second: one leader per identical in-flight call. Correctness work — upstream quota, cache fills — is paid once per unique call, not once per client asking; N identical concurrent requests yield one upstream call and one cache fill. Third: the follower response must be byte-perfect. Followers don't share the leader's response buffer: Multiplexer.Close (erpc/multiplexer.go :36, using sync.Once) clones the response once per follower and CopyResponseForRequest (common/response.go :615) rewrites the JSON-RPC id byte-for-byte; a copyWg wait group (copyWg.Add(1) at :3086, copyWg.Wait() in cleanupMultiplexer :3162) guarantees no follower reads a buffer freed by cleanup.

Identity is where chains disagree. SVM cannot reuse the EVM cache hash because CacheHash() lowercases params, which would collapse distinct case-sensitive base58 addresses; EVM keys on req.CacheHash() while SVM keys on svmRequestKey (chapter 13). The choice is made in Network.multiplexKey (networks.go:3043) and regression-tested by TestSvmCache_RequestKey_PreservesBase58Case in architecture/svm/json_rpc_cache_test.go:240. Multiplexing is on by default (MultiplexingEnabled, common/config.go:2266).

Edge cases. 1. SVM base58 case sensitivity: the shared hasher lowercases params, which would wrongly merge distinct addresses; SVM uses its own request key. 2. Buffer lifetime across followers: cleanup waits on copyWg so no follower reads a freed response buffer. 3. Client disconnect doesn't abort bookkeeping: the async cache write, shadow-upstream fan-out, and skip-triggered head polls all outlive the response/caller. 4. The multiplexer runs before the cache read. 5. No new magic timeouts: background work hangs off existing failsafe/HTTP budgets.

erpc/multiplexer.gotype Multiplexer (:12), NewMultiplexer (:29), Close (:36)Leader/follower rendezvous object with sync.Once close.

Metrics: erpc_network_multiplexed_request_total (labels project, network, category, finality, user, agent_name) fires when a request is multiplexed (follower); erpc_network_static_response_served_total counts canned replies served without contacting an upstream.

4. Request tracing

eRPC exports OpenTelemetry traces, and its central convention is that span names are function names — a trace in an OTLP backend is a direct index into the Go source tree. Two span tiers exist: always-on StartSpan spans and StartDetailSpan spans that additionally require tracing.detailed: true (common/tracing_util.go :32, :41). The span infrastructure lives in common/tracing_util.go (StartHTTPServerSpan :67, StartRequestHandleSpan :155–175, InjectHTTPResponseTraceContext :58) with the force-trace attribute and sampler wrapper in common/tracing_core.go (:29, :248).

The span hierarchy for one cache-missing, hedged eth_getBlockByNumber call:

Http.ReceivedRequest → Http.ReadBody (detail) → Http.ParseRequests (detail)
→ Request.Handle → Project.Forward (detail) → RateLimiter.DoLimit →
Network.Forward → PolicyEngine.GetOrdered (detail) → Cache.Get →
Network.forwardAttempt → Consensus.Run → Upstream.Forward →
HttpJsonRpcClient.sendSingleRequest → Cache.Set → HttpServer.WriteResponse (detail)

Walk one call through four scenarios. Cache hit: six functions, zero upstreams — a hit never calls Cache.Set. Cold read + hedge: Cache.Get misses, the policy engine orders upstreams, the failsafe executor fires a hedge at an adaptive delay; the losing leg dies with ErrUpstreamHedgeCancelled and the response carries X-ERPC-Upstream-Hedges: 1 (writeCounterHeaders, http_server.go:1225, :1230). Missing-data retry: the upstream returns -32014, classified reason=missing_data, the executor waits about one EMA block time and retries on another upstream, capped by dataUnavailableCapReached (network_executor.go:385). Consensus: Consensus.Run fans out three consensus_slot attempts in parallel; two identical responses short-circuit the third, and the analyzer goroutine keeps draining after the response returns.

Before the network response finishes, ExecState().Apply (common/exec_state.go:325) stamps execution.* counters and upstreams.tried/outcomes/reasons/durations_ms/won slices onto the Network.Forward span, so one span answers "which upstreams, why, and who won." A batch produces N Request.Handle spans — one per element goroutine — with no batch-level parent beyond Http.ParseRequests.

KeyDefaultNotes
tracing.enabledfalseFully off until configured.
tracing.protocolgrpcgrpc or http.
tracing.endpointlocalhost:4317 (grpc); http://localhost:4318 (http)OTLP collector.
tracing.sampleRate1.0Head-sampling fraction [0,1].
tracing.detailedfalseUnlocks StartDetailSpan spans.
tracing.serviceNameerpcOTel service name.
tracing.headers, tls, resourceAttributesnilExporter auth/TLS, extra resource attributes.
tracing.forceTraceMatchersnil{network, method} wildcard patterns force-sampled (OR within a field, AND across).

Per-request, X-ERPC-Force-Trace: true or ?force-trace=true forces a trace past the sampler — but force-tracing does not unlock detail spans; the tier split still requires tracing.detailed: true.

Timeouts are contexts with causes, not checked flags. The executor sets ErrDynamicTimeoutExceeded on the context at network_executor.go:178; the deepest upstream learns the remaining budget the same way — one mechanism, visible end-to-end in the trace as cancellations with causes.

Edge cases. 1. Auth is invisible in traces — strategy evaluation and its rate permit emit logs/metrics but no span; a Request.Handle → Project.Forward jump is normal. 2. Hedge losers end in ErrUpstreamHedgeCancelled — filter them, don't read them as upstream failure. 3. Cache.Set runs on a detached 10s context carrying the Network.Forward span context, so it appears as a late child span; a client disconnect never aborts it. 4. Recovered panics surface in erpc_unexpected_panic_total (labels scope, extra, error), e.g. scope="request-handler" or scope="cache-set".

5. Finality & caching

CDN-style wall-clock TTL caching is wrong for blockchains. Below the finalized tip, history is immutable — a TTL there wastes free correctness. Above it, no answer survives a re-org — a long TTL serves wrong answers. eRPC's solution: every response is tagged with one of four finality states — finalized, unfinalized, realtime, unknown — and cache policies match per bucket (common/data.go:10–27; finalized is the zero value). Finalized data is stored with no TTL; tip data lives under short TTLs. The key insight is that there is no re-org invalidation path at all: "latest" tags are interpolated to concrete block numbers before hashing (architecture/evm/json_rpc.go resolveBlockTagToHex :58, NormalizeHttpJsonRpc :92), so each new block produces a new cache key of the form method:sha256(params) (common/json_rpc.go:1398), and orphaned entries simply die when their TTL expires.

Realtime tip data gets an age guard. shouldAcceptCachedResult (architecture/evm/json_rpc_cache.go:926) rejects cached entries whose block timestamp has aged past the policy TTL, with a defaultRealtimeColdStartTTL = 2s (:917) bound when block time is unknown:

func (c *EvmJsonRpcCache) shouldAcceptCachedResult(
	ctx context.Context,
	req *common.NormalizedRequest,
	jrr *common.JsonRpcResponse,
	policy *data.CachePolicy,
) bool {
	// Only apply age guard for realtime finality.
	// Finalized/unfinalized/unknown data is immutable - a block from 2022 is still valid today.
	// The age guard is only meaningful for realtime queries (eth_gasPrice, latest block, etc.)
	// where users expect fresh data that changes with each new block.
	finality := req.Finality(ctx)
	if finality != common.DataFinalityStateRealtime {
		return true
	}

	// Resolve the realtime age limit from the policy TTL: a fixed value, or one
	// derived from the network's estimated block time (object form). ...
	effectiveTTL := policy.ResolveTTL(networkBlockTime(req), defaultRealtimeColdStartTTL)
	if effectiveTTL <= 0 {
		return true
	}

	// ... (block timestamp extracted from response, or falling back to the
	// serving connector's reported latest-block timestamp)

	// Calculate the age of the block
	now := time.Now().Unix()
	age := time.Duration(now-blockTimestamp) * time.Second

	// Check if the age exceeds the TTL
	if age > effectiveTTL {
		// ... debug log + MetricCacheGetAgeGuardRejectTotal; then return false
	}

— architecture/evm/json_rpc_cache.go:926–986 (verbatim, trimmed).

Writes are async and guarded. The cache write is a fire-and-forget goroutine with a 10-second budget (networks.go:2426, 10s at :2449), and shouldCacheResponse (json_rpc_cache.go:1158) rejects errors, oversized items, stale realtime tips from lagging upstreams, and — always — empty results for not-yet-produced blocks (emptyResultBeyondConfidence, architecture/evm/common.go:62), which would otherwise be lies-in-wait. Policy matching lives in data/cache_policy.go: MatchesForSet (:82), MatchesForGet (:124), ResolveTTL (:293). Finality is memoized per request in common/request.go:1123 and common/response.go:144.

Below the finalized tip, data can never change, so cache it forever — a TTL there only throws away free correctness. Above it, every answer is provisional, so every entry needs an expiry. The horizon, not the clock, decides.

Edge cases. 1. Writes require exact finality equality; reads are asymmetric — finalized reads also consult unfinalized policies, never the reverse (entries written before finalization stay findable). 2. unknown finality iterates all policies in config order — put the fastest storage first. 3. Non-numeric tags short-circuit to realtime; tx-hash methods (e.g. eth_getTransactionReceipt) get their block ref from the response body, which is what makes their cache hits classifiable. 4. A future-block empty result is never cached regardless of empty behavior. 5. The age guard falls back to the connector-reported head for methods without a timestamp (eth_blockNumber, eth_gasPrice, eth_getLogs) and fails open if neither exists. 6. safe/pending tags pass through untranslated — eRPC doesn't track the needed state honestly. 7. A client disconnect never aborts the async cache write.

Metrics: erpc_cache_get_success_hit_total, erpc_cache_get_success_miss_total (reason connector_miss/connector_error/ttl_rejected/empty_result), erpc_cache_get_skipped_total, erpc_cache_get_age_guard_reject_total, erpc_cache_set_success_total, erpc_cache_set_skipped_total.

6. Block availability & the upstream sweep

Upstreams see the chain at different heights; asking a node for block N it doesn't have yields null. eRPC's answer is to know each upstream's serving range — evm.blockAvailability lower/upper bounds, resolved in upstream/upstream.go:1161–1168 — plus a live head from the state poller, and to gate dispatch per-upstream before sending. The gate is Network.checkUpstreamBlockAvailability (erpc/networks.go:2869, call site :2194):

func (n *Network) checkUpstreamBlockAvailability(ctx context.Context, u common.Upstream, req *common.NormalizedRequest, method string) (error, bool) {
	if n.cfg.Architecture != common.ArchitectureEvm {
		return nil, false
	}
	// Range methods (eth_getLogs, trace_filter, arbtrace_filter) enforce block
	// availability via their own range-aware pre-forward hooks; ...
	if methodHasDedicatedRangeAvailabilityHook(method) {
		return nil, false
	}
	// Explicit method/network enforceBlockAvailability:false is an operator opt-out.
	if n.blockAvailabilityExplicitlyDisabled(method) {
		return nil, false
	}
	eu, ok := u.(common.EvmUpstream)
	if !ok {
		return nil, false
	}
	// Resolve the upstream's configured serving range ... Unbounded on
	// both sides means the upstream advertises no restriction → nothing to enforce.
	minBound, maxBound := eu.EvmBlockAvailabilityBounds()
	if minBound == math.MinInt64 && maxBound == math.MaxInt64 {
		return nil, false
	}

	// ... (block number resolved from req.EvmBlockNumber(), with defensive
	// extraction fallback; unknown → fail-open, return nil, false)

	// Below the configured lower bound: the upstream genuinely cannot serve this
	// historical block (e.g. pruned). Not retryable on this upstream.
	if minBound != math.MinInt64 && bn < minBound {
		telemetry.MetricUpstreamStaleLowerBound.WithLabelValues(
			n.projectId, eu.VendorName(), n.Label(), eu.Id(), method, common.AvailbilityConfidenceBlockHead.String(),
		).Inc()
		latestBlock, finalizedBlock := n.upstreamHeads(eu)
		return common.NewErrUpstreamBlockUnavailable(eu.Id(), bn, latestBlock, finalizedBlock), false
	}

	// Above the configured upper bound. Classify retryability by distance to the live
	// head: a block just ahead of the head (e.g. upper=latestBlockMinus:0) may become
	// serveable shortly, so it is retryable within MaxRetryableBlockDistance.
	if maxBound != math.MaxInt64 && bn > maxBound {
		telemetry.MetricUpstreamStaleUpperBound.WithLabelValues(
			n.projectId, eu.VendorName(), n.Label(), eu.Id(), method, common.AvailbilityConfidenceBlockHead.String(),
		).Inc()
		latestBlock, finalizedBlock := n.upstreamHeads(eu)
		blockErr := common.NewErrUpstreamBlockUnavailable(eu.Id(), bn, latestBlock, finalizedBlock)
		if bn > latestBlock && latestBlock > 0 {
			return blockErr, bn-latestBlock <= n.maxRetryableBlockDistance()
		}
		return blockErr, false
	}

	return nil, false
}

— erpc/networks.go:2869–2937 (verbatim, trimmed).

Below the lower bound is a terminal skip — pruned history never returns. Above the upper bound is a retryable skip while the block is within maxRetryableBlockDistance of the upstream's live head — the default is max(128, 60s ÷ EMA block time) (common/defaults.go), a distance that scales with chain speed so "one minute of progress" means the same thing everywhere. A retryable skip fires an async PollLatestBlockNumber (10s, debounce-coalesced; default poller debounce 5s, DefaultEvmStatePollerDebounce at common/defaults.go:2364) so the retry sees a fresh head. If the node returns empty anyway, the executor classifies it as "not yet data" (block_unavailable / empty_result / missing_data via shouldRetryWithReason, network_executor.go:396) and waits exactly EMA block time × blockUnavailableDelayMultiplier (default 1.0) — betting the block appears within about one block. Blocks beyond every upstream's head short-circuit to a truthful synthesized null (tryShortCircuitFutureBlock :853) with no dispatch and no rate-limit permit.

Every "can't tell" branch fails open: non-EVM network, unresolvable block number (block-hash lookups), cold poller, or no bounds → the request proceeds. And catch-up retries (emptyResultMaxAttempts) are a separate budget from maxAttempts (genuine-error failover): genuine errors use exponential backoff, not the catch-up path.

Availability gating is a latency and quota optimization; it must never become the reason a serveable request fails.

Edge cases. 1. Deliberately no implicit "block > latestBlock" head check in the gate — it raced the poller on fast chains (issue #934); tip-awareness lives in the short-circuit and enforceHighestBlock. 2. The short-circuit compares against the MAX head across eligible upstreams, not the majority served tip, so it can never null out a block the most-ahead upstream has. 3. Range methods (eth_getLogs, trace_filter, arbtrace_filter) are exempt from the gate — they have their own range-aware hook. 4. Syncing upstreams are excluded from head computation (4 consecutive syncing=false required; one true resets the counter; FullySyncedThreshold = 4 in architecture/evm/evm_state_poller.go:25). 5. Catch-up volume on finalized data is a red flag; a non-zero baseline on tip data is normal tip-racing.

Metrics: erpc_upstream_stale_upper_bound_total, erpc_upstream_stale_lower_bound_total, erpc_upstream_request_errors_total (skips logged severity="info"), erpc_network_retry_attempt_total{reason=...}, erpc_network_data_unavailable_wait_seconds, erpc_network_dynamic_block_time_milliseconds.

7. Failsafe, in depth

Network-scope failsafes compose as a fixed-order nesting doll — timeout(consensus(retry(hedge(upstream-sweep)))) — with every layer optional and matched per (method, finality, request kind), but never reordered. The composition is decided in networkExecutor.Run (erpc/network_executor.go:164):

// Composition per spec §11.2:
//   - When consensus is configured: consensus(retry(hedge(tryOneUpstream)))
//     where tryOneUpstream picks ONE upstream (via NextUpstream) per slot.
//   - When consensus is NOT configured: retry(hedge(runUpstreamSweep))
//     where runUpstreamSweep tries all upstreams within one execution.
//
// ...
	if e.HasConsensus() && e.consensus != nil && !skipConsensus && !singleDispatchWrite {
		slotInner := func(slotCtx context.Context, slotReq *common.NormalizedRequest) (*common.NormalizedResponse, error) {
			return e.runRetryHedge(slotCtx, slotReq, tryOneUpstream)
		}
		return e.consensus.Run(ctx, req, slotInner)
	}

	// Non-consensus branch: retry(hedge(runUpstreamSweep)).
	return e.runRetryHedge(ctx, req, runUpstreamSweep)
}

func (e *networkExecutor) runRetryHedge(
	ctx context.Context,
	req *common.NormalizedRequest,
	inner func(ctx context.Context, req *common.NormalizedRequest) (*common.NormalizedResponse, error),
) (*common.NormalizedResponse, error) {
	hedgeWrapped := func(ctx context.Context) (*common.NormalizedResponse, error) {
		return e.runHedge(ctx, req, inner)
	}
	return e.runRetry(ctx, req, hedgeWrapped)
}

— erpc/network_executor.go:156–225 (verbatim, trimmed).

The real design problem is the three-way classification after every attempt: real data → return; empty (maybe not-yet-data) → wait ~one EMA block and retry under a small cap; error → retryable gets fast backoff + upstream rotation, deterministic errors return immediately. Retrying "empty" like a 502 would hammer upstreams; waiting a block for a 502 would add pointless latency — delay policy follows the failure mode. The classification lives in shouldRetryWithReason (:396) with reasons missing_data, block_unavailable, retryable_error, empty_result, pending_tx, execution_exception_retryable, capped by dataUnavailableCapReached (:385). The hedge race (runHedge :589) rejects fast-but-empty answers unless the method is in emptyResultAccept (for eth_getLogs, eth_call, etc., null is a legitimate answer); the keep-rule at :677 is kept = !IsRetryableTowardNetwork(err).

Scope rules are enforced by validation, not convention: NewNetworkExecutor (:71) rejects a circuit breaker at network scope, and upstream/upstream_executor.go:47 rejects consensus at upstream scope — both are startup errors. The circuit breaker lives one scope down, per upstream: a ring buffer of 80 outcomes that opens at 20 failures, with a half-open trial after 5 minutes (failsafe/breaker.go); hedges, probes, and cancellations never move it (upstreamBreakerOutcome, upstream_executor.go:398).

PolicyKey defaults
retrymaxAttempts: 3 (network injected default 5; upstream scope 1), delay: 0, backoffFactor: 1.2, backoffMaxDelay: 3s, emptyResultMaxAttempts: 2, blockUnavailableDelayMultiplier: 1.0.
hedgeminDelay: 100ms, maxDelay: 999s, maxCount: 1; adaptive delay = clamp(quantile of method latency + base, min, max).
timeoutLifecycle-scoped, not per-attempt; network default 120s, upstream default 60s.
circuitBreakerRing capacity 80, open at 20 failures, halfOpenAfter: 5m, 8 of 200 trial successes to re-close.

Edge cases. 1. Write methods (eth_sendRawTransaction, SVM sendTransaction) are never hedged — non-idempotent broadcasts must not fan out. 2. emptyResultAccept inverts empty-as-failure for methods where null is canonical. 3. Permanently-absent data (skipped slot) returns no-retry immediately — only genuinely-not-yet data waits. 4. A hedge timer pool exists because time.NewTimer showed up in production heap profiles; cold start (no latency quantile) falls back to the min delay. 5. Syncing-and-empty counts as a breaker failure; cancellations/skips are "ignore". 6. The lifecycle timeout bounds all retries/hedges together, not per attempt.

Metrics: erpc_network_retry_attempt_total, erpc_network_data_unavailable_wait_seconds, erpc_network_hedge_winner_total, erpc_network_hedged_request_total, erpc_network_timeout_fired_total, erpc_upstream_breaker_state_change_total.

8. Consensus

One provider can return a wrong answer indistinguishable from a right one, so consensus fans one request out to maxParticipants upstreams (default 5), groups responses by canonical hash, and declares a winner when agreementThreshold (default 2) distinct upstreams agree. Each slot runs the inner doll retry(hedge(one upstream)) with a distinct upstream and its own cancellable context. The executor is consensus/executor.go: Run (:120), executeConsensus (:182), runAnalyzer (:359), with analysis in consensus/analysis.go (classifyAndHashResponse :469, dedupeByUpstream :201) and rules in consensus/rules.go (consensusRules :42, shortCircuitRules :858).

Four insights carry the design. (a) Infrastructure errors never vote. Timeouts, 5xx, and connection resets carry no information about the truth, so only data-vs-data dissent is meaningful; when no group can prove agreement, the rule table falls through to an explicit ErrConsensusDispute or ErrConsensusLowParticipants, never to a random pick. (b) Responses are deduped by upstream ID (dedupeByUpstream) so retry/hedge reselection can't double-vote. (c) The unassailable_lead short-circuit releases the caller the moment the winner can't change — winner non-empty, count ≥ threshold, lead over the runner-up ≥ responses still outstanding — then cancels stragglers, while the analyzer keeps collecting so every vote reaches misbehavior tracking:

// shouldShortCircuit decides if remaining requests can be safely cancelled.
// This happens if one group's lead over the second-place group is greater
// than the number of remaining responses.
func (e *executor) shouldShortCircuit(winner *slotResult, analysis *consensusAnalysis) (string, bool) {
	// A composition dispute is provisional while more responses can still
	// arrive: a later response may join the leading group (or grow another
	// group) and satisfy the minAgreement quota. Never cancel remaining
	// participants because of it — the final pass after collection decides.
	if winner != nil && winner.Error != nil && analysis.hasRemaining() &&
		common.HasErrorCode(winner.Error, common.ErrCodeConsensusCompositionDispute) {
		return "", false
	}
	for _, rule := range shortCircuitRules {
		if rule.Condition(winner, analysis) {
			return rule.Reason, true
		}
	}
	return "", false
}
	{
		Description: "winner meets agreement threshold, is non-empty, and lead is unassailable (no possible tie with remaining)",
		Reason:      "unassailable_lead",
		Condition: func(w *slotResult, a *consensusAnalysis) bool {
			// ... (guards: preferHighestValueFor, preferLargerResponses,
			// preferNonEmpty-with-empty-leader all veto short-circuiting)
			if best == nil || best.ResponseType != ResponseTypeNonEmpty || best.Count < a.config.agreementThreshold {
				return false
			}
			// Compute second best among valid groups (non-infrastructure)
			secondCount := 0
			for _, g := range a.getValidGroups() {
				if g.Hash == best.Hash {
					continue
				}
				if g.Count > secondCount {
					secondCount = g.Count
				}
			}
			// Raw collected count, not deduplicated votes: a deduplicated
			// duplicate consumed a slot and can no longer arrive.
			remaining := a.config.maxParticipants - a.collectedResponses
			// Without size preference, allow potential ties to short-circuit once threshold is met
			// and the lead is unassailable by the number of remaining responses.
			leadOverSecond := best.Count - secondCount
			return leadOverSecond >= remaining
		},
	},

— consensus/executor.go:822–840 and consensus/rules.go:910–956 (verbatim, trimmed).

(d) Punishment requires provable dissent against a >50% data majority, enforced by a per-upstream token bucket (disputeThreshold per disputeWindow) → cordon for sitOutPenalty via Cordon("*", ...); it is off by default. Caller latency and bookkeeping are decoupled via a size-1 buffered outcome channel (outcomeCh :258): the analyzer keeps collecting after the caller leaves so every vote reaches misbehavior tracking. Disputes resolve to HTTP 409 with a participant table (common/errors.go:2779–2811).

KeyDefaultEffect
consensus.maxParticipants5Upstreams to fan out to.
consensus.agreementThreshold2Distinct upstreams that must agree on one response hash.
consensus.preferLargerResponsestruePrefer larger bodies; disables ALL short-circuiting (callers pay the wait caps).
consensus.preferNonEmptytruePrefer non-empty over empty/error in dispute resolution.
consensus.maxWaitOnResultadaptive p50, clamp [5ms, 1s]Cap after the first non-empty response.
consensus.maxWaitOnEmptyadaptive p90, clamp [50ms, 2s]Cap after the first response of any kind.
consensus.disputeBehaviorreturnErrorWhat happens when no group meets the threshold.
consensus.punishMisbehavioroff unless setExample: {disputeThreshold: 2, disputeWindow: 5m, sitOutPenalty: 10m}.

Edge cases. 1. Skip via X-ERPC-Skip-Consensus: true, ?skip-consensus=true, or directiveDefaults.skipConsensus. 2. Single-dispatch writes (e.g. Solana requestAirdrop) skip consensus — one call must not mint N airdrops. 3. unassailable_lead is disabled under preferLargerResponses: true (the default), so callers normally pay the wait caps. 4. Composition quota failure becomes ErrConsensusCompositionDispute, which no dispute behavior may bypass. 5. Errored dissent is tracked separately (erpc_consensus_upstream_errors_total) and is never misbehavior; cordon requires a consensus group > validParticipants/2 — a 1-1-1 split punishes no one. 6. Default ignoreFields strip blockTimestamp and SVM context.slot/context.apiVersion — fields honest nodes legitimately differ on. 7. eth_sendRawTransaction returns the first non-empty response immediately (broadcast mode).

Metrics: erpc_consensus_total, erpc_consensus_duration_seconds, erpc_consensus_short_circuit_total, erpc_consensus_responses_collected, erpc_consensus_agreement_count, erpc_consensus_misbehavior_detected_total, erpc_consensus_upstream_errors_total, erpc_consensus_upstream_punished_total, erpc_consensus_wait_capped_total, erpc_consensus_cancellations_total.

9. Health & selection

eRPC's ranking of upstreams is never read from config — it is continuously re-derived from live measurement. Every upstream attempt writes into a per-(upstream, method, finality) rolling health window: one minute split into 10 rotating 6-second sub-buckets (health/rolling.go, rollingBuckets = 10). Latency goes into a DDSketch at 1% relative accuracy (health/quantile.go) only for success-like outcomes — responses, EVM reverts, hedge-loser lower bounds (Tracker.RecordUpstreamDuration, health/tracker.go:974) — so a fast-failing upstream can't win "fastest". Errors, throttles, and misbehaviors go into rolling counters; block-head lag is stored as state (networkHighest − upstreamHighest, SetLatestBlockNumber :1392) plus an EMA of chain block time that converts block lag into wall-clock seconds (returns 0 until enough samples — deliberate fresh-boot quiet).

Independently of the request path, a per-(network, method, finality, boundary) Slot goroutine (internal/policy/slot.go) ticks every 15 seconds: it snapshots tracker metrics, runs a JavaScript policy on a pooled sobek runtime with a 100ms budget, and atomically swaps the published order (and excluded set) into a cache (:318). Request handling never waits — Network.Forward reads the last published slice with one atomic.Pointer load via Engine.GetOrderedInLane (internal/policy/engine.go:368). A failed or timed-out eval keeps the previous order (:256), so a broken policy can never stall routing. The first tick runs synchronously at registration (~:316); before that, registration order is used.

The default embedded policy (internal/policy/default_policy.js, trimmed):

(upstreams, ctx) =>
  upstreams
    .removeCordoned()
    // Errors / throttle: drop upstreams that are clearly broken, gated
    // on samplesAbove(10) so a single failed call can't evict a fresh-
    // pod upstream. Thresholds are loose — failsafe (retry/hedge/
    // consensus) already absorbs occasional failures.
    .excludeIf(all(samplesAbove(10), errorRateAbove(0.7)))
    .excludeIf(all(samplesAbove(10), throttleRateAbove(0.4)))
    // Block-head lag: drop if behind tip by ≥16 blocks or ≥30s.
    .excludeIf(any(blockNumberLagAbove(16), blockSecondsLagAbove(30)))
    // Outage safety net: if everyone failed the health excludes, fall
    // back to the raw set rather than failing closed.
    .whenEmpty(() => upstreams)
    // Tier split: prefer non-fallback; fall back to tier:fallback if no
    // primary survives.
    .preferTag('!tier:fallback', { minHealthy: 1, fallback: 'tier:fallback' })
    // Rank survivors by p70 latency.
    .sortByScore(PREFER_FASTEST)
    // Hold the primary stable across ticks unless a meaningfully better
    // option exists for ≥30s.
    .stickyPrimary({ hysteresis: 0.30, minSwitchInterval: '30s' })
    .probeExcluded({ sampleRate: 0.1, minSamples: 10, minSamplesWindow: '60s', maxConcurrent: 4, timeout: '10s' })

— internal/policy/default_policy.js:1–63 (verbatim, trimmed; the latency-exclusion stage and a long comment block are omitted).

The scoring formula (stdlib at internal/policy/stdlib/stdlib.js:741): score = overall / (1 + Σ metricᵢ × weightᵢ), higher wins, with weights latency p70 × 15, error × 4, throttle × 4, misbehavior × 2, head lag × 1. Two stability mechanisms dominate: hysteresis — a challenger must beat the incumbent's score by 1.30× and 30s must have elapsed since the last switch — and probing — 10% of real requests are mirrored to excluded upstreams (internal/policy/prober.go) so they accumulate fresh samples; re-admission is just the exclusion predicates no longer tripping. Writes are never probed.

Edge cases. 1. Quantile fed only on success-like outcomes; hedge-cancel is recorded as a lower-bound duration. 2. BlockHeadLagSeconds returns 0 until enough block-time samples — seconds-based lag gates stay quiet on fresh boot by design. 3. Eval throw/timeout keeps the previous order, surfaced via consecutiveFails + erpc_selection_eval_errors_total{kind} (timeout/throw/invalid_return). 4. Exclusion predicates require sample floors (error gate ≥10 samples) so one failed call can't evict a fresh pod. 5. Probe feed is a 256-slot channel; when full, publishes drop (erpc_selection_probe_dropped_total) — the request path never blocks. 6. Probe overruns count as failures; writes never mirrored. 7. erpc_selection_excluded_seconds > 600s = stuck-excluded alert threshold.

Metrics: erpc_selection_position, erpc_selection_score, erpc_selection_eligible_upstreams, erpc_selection_eval_duration_seconds, erpc_selection_eval_errors_total, erpc_selection_rejection_total, erpc_selection_exclusion_total, erpc_selection_shadow_exclusion_total, erpc_selection_excluded_seconds, erpc_selection_readmit_total, erpc_selection_readmit_age_seconds, erpc_selection_primary_switch_total, erpc_selection_sticky_hold_total, erpc_selection_probe_requests_total, erpc_selection_probe_errors_total, erpc_selection_probe_skipped_total, erpc_selection_probe_dropped_total, erpc_upstream_block_head_lag, erpc_upstream_cordoned, erpc_upstream_request_duration_seconds, erpc_upstream_selection_total.

10. EVM translation

Clients speak in moving references — "latest", 175k-block eth_getLogs ranges — but caches and upstreams need concrete, servable requests. eRPC rewrites requests before downstream subsystems see them, through per-method translation hooks. Three rewrites matter. (a) Tag interpolation: resolvable block tags (latest, finalized) become concrete hex at the top of Network.Forward (architecture/evm/json_rpc.go resolveBlockTagToHex :58, NormalizeHttpJsonRpc :92), so identical logical reads share one cache key. Unresolvable tags (safe, pending, earliest, hashes) pass through untouched — fail-open beats fail-guessed, because a guessed translation poisons cache entries. (b) Proactive getLogs splitting: oversized eth_getLogs ranges are sliced into contiguous chunks, each a first-class request re-entering Network.Forward (splitEthGetLogsRequest, architecture/evm/eth_get_logs.go:583; executeGetLogsSubRequests :696) with its own cache entry, bounded by a semaphore — then merged in order by a streaming writer (GetLogsMultiResponseWriter :460). No special bulk path, just composition. (c) Reactive bisection: happens once when an upstream refuses with -32012 (block range → address list → topics[0]); sub-requests carry ParentRequestId so they're never re-split (JsonRpcErrorEvmLargeRange, common/errors.go:2341).

eth_chainId is answered from config without touching an upstream (architecture/evm/eth_chainId.go:25). The governing config: upstreams[].evm.getLogsAutoSplittingRangeThreshold (default project template 5000; 0 = opt out), getLogsMaxAllowedRange (30000), getLogsSplitConcurrency (10), getLogsMaxAllowedAddresses/getLogsMaxAllowedTopics (0 = unlimited), getLogsMaxResponseBytes (0 = unbounded), networks[].evm.getLogsSplitOnError (true).

✂️ Bound the work, not the answer. Hard caps reject requests (30,000-block range, merged-bytes budget); thresholds split them — and only an upstream's own "too large" triggers bisection, never eRPC's caps.

Edge cases. 1. Unresolvable tags pass through — fail-open beats fail-guessed. 2. Hard-cap violations return HTTP 413 and never trigger reactive splitting. 3. Effective threshold = min positive upstream threshold, capped by max range. 4. The merged response is fromCache only if every chunk hit. 5. Byte budget checked before cloning, so oversized chunks are never duplicated. 6. Bisect is one-shot; halves carry ParentRequestId and skip the hooks. 7. Empty getLogs results are normalized to [] (normalizeEmptyArrayResponse, architecture/evm/common.go:91) so "no logs" caches as data.

Metrics: erpc_network_evm_get_logs_range_requested (histogram), erpc_network_evm_get_logs_forced_splits_total, erpc_network_evm_get_logs_split_success_total, erpc_network_evm_get_logs_split_failure_total, erpc_cache_evm_get_logs_range (histogram), erpc_upstream_request_total with composite = logs-split-proactive / logs-split-on-error.

11. Errors

Every upstream vendor speaks its own dialect of failure: Alchemy reuses code 3 for two different errors; Solana's -32005 means NodeUnhealthy while eRPC uses the same number for rate limits; errors ride in HTTP 400s or 200s. eRPC normalizes every raw wire error into one typed taxonomy:

type ErrorCode string

type BaseError struct {
	Code    ErrorCode              `json:"code,omitempty"`
	Message string                 `json:"message,omitempty"`
	Cause   error                  `json:"cause,omitempty"`
	Details map[string]interface{} `json:"details,omitempty"`
}

type StandardError interface {
	HasCode(...ErrorCode) bool
	CodeChain() string
	DeepestMessage() string
	DeepSearch(key string) interface{}
	GetCause() error
	Base() *BaseError
	MarshalZerologObject(v *zerolog.Event)
	Error() string
}

— common/errors.go:185–203 (verbatim).

Details carries behavioral flags (retryableTowardNetwork, permanentMissingData), and the key insight is that retryability is structural, not configured — no retryable-error config and no per-method retry-code table exists; policies query the flags (IsRetryableTowardNetwork :2550, IsRetryableTowardsUpstream :2636, IsPermanentlyMissingData :2616) and never parse messages or wire codes. The pipeline: (1) the HTTP client calls the injected JsonRpcErrorExtractor on any JSON-RPC error or HTTP >299 (clients/http_json_rpc_client.go:924); (2) the owning vendor's GetVendorSpecificErrorIfAny hook fires before generic matchers (25 vendors implement it; Alchemy disambiguates code 3 via IsMissingDataError, architecture/evm/util.go:26); (3) the architecture normalizer (architecture/evm/error_normalizer.go, architecture/svm/error_normalizer.go, gRPC twin) maps the remainder, falling back to ErrEndpointServerSideException with raw-code passthrough; (4) decision gates (shouldRetry, shouldRetryWithReason, hedge keep-rules, breaker outcome) read flags; (5) if everything fails, the exhausted bundle collapses via TranslateToJsonRpcException (common/json_rpc.go:1704) into one deterministic verdict — dominant cause chosen by orderCauses (:916), unanimous block-unavailable gating -32014 (isBlockUnavailableVerdict :1684) — rendered as JSON-RPC inside HTTP 200 by design (non-200 is reserved for transport conditions).

{"code": -32014, "message": "all upstream attempts failed (2 upstream missing data, 1 upstream timeout)"}

— rendered over HTTP 200, by design (erpc/http_server.go:1840–1860 reserves 400/401/404/429 for transport-level conditions).

Edge cases. 1. Alchemy code 3 is two errors — IsMissingDataError splits data-availability from genuine reverts. 2. -32005 collision: only local rate limits remap to -32000 on SVM requests; native upstream -32005 passes through with its Agave meaning (NodeUnhealthy). 3. Causeless ErrUpstreamsExhausted is terminal — no automatic re-sweep. 4. Bundles: any-child retryable; the predicate never descends joined multi-error wrappers via DeepSearch. 5. SVM permanent-missing codes -32007/-32009 skip the wait-and-retry loop. 6. Non-retryable writes never retry at upstream scope. 7. The -32014 verdict is unanimity-gated across all non-skipped causes. 8. Dominance tally excludes ErrUpstreamRequestSkipped and ErrEndpointUnsupported. 9. RetryEmpty/RetryPending only widen; they can't make a structurally non-retryable error retryable.

Metrics: erpc_upstream_attempt_outcome_total (13-outcome enum), erpc_upstream_selection_total (reason: primary/retry/hedge/consensus_slot/sweep), erpc_network_retry_attempt_total (6 reasons), erpc_upstream_request_errors_total (+severity).

12. Metrics

All erpc_* series live in one registry (telemetry/metrics.go, built with promauto), and each metric family fires at exactly one decision point in the request path — a selection reason, a retry reason, an attempt outcome. Counters are denominators: real health is rates and ratios, not raw counts. Four structural facts explain most surprises:

  1. Absent is not zero. A cache HIT emits zero upstream series — they're absent, not 0.
  2. A cancelled hedge-loser is an attempt outcome, never an error. Hedge churn shows up only in erpc_network_hedge_discards_total.
  3. The async cache SET fires after the 200 leaves, so client latency never pays for bookkeeping.
  4. The error label is ErrorFingerprint (common/errors.go:117) — sanitized, 256-char cap — to bound cardinality; high-cardinality handles go through CounterHandle/ObserverHandle so the health tracker sweeps stale label sets.

The top-ten misreads, from the metrics deep dive:

  1. erpc_upstream_block_head_large_rollback is a sticky gauge — it never resets, so rate() is meaningless.
  2. Served-tip regression/trajectory metrics count transitions, not evaluations.
  3. erpc_network_served_tip_lag_blocks absent in default MAX mode — not 0.
  4. erpc_rate_limiter_budget_decision_total is deprecated.
  5. The finality label is dual-meaning (head axis vs DataFinalityState).
  6. cache_executor_attempt_total{outcome="success"} ≠ cache hit — it means "answered within budget".
  7. Pre-dispatch vs post-resolution finality labels can make misbehavior ratios exceed 100%.
  8. Hedge attempts are excluded from health-scoring counters — watch erpc_network_hedge_discards_total.
  9. Catch-up retries have a normal non-zero baseline (judge by pressure trend, not raw counts).
  10. erpc_consensus_responses_collected is a histogram of counts (buckets 1–10), not a duration.

Core families to know: erpc_network_request_received_total, erpc_network_successful_request_total, erpc_network_failed_request_total, erpc_network_request_duration_seconds, erpc_network_hedged_request_total, erpc_network_hedge_discards_total, erpc_network_hedge_winner_total, erpc_network_hedge_delay_seconds, erpc_network_data_unavailable_wait_seconds, erpc_cache_get_success_hit/miss_total, erpc_cache_set_success_total, erpc_cache_executor_attempt_total, erpc_consensus_total, the erpc_selection_* family, erpc_rate_limits_total, erpc_upstream_misbehavior_total, erpc_upstream_breaker_state_change_total, erpc_auth_failed_total, erpc_shadow_response_*, erpc_unexpected_panic_total.

13. Architecture: SVM (Solana)

eRPC's core promise is that one pipeline — caching, failsafe executors, consensus, upstream selection — serves any chain without naming one. Solana is the proof: everything chain-specific lives in a single Go package (architecture/svm/) behind six hooks on one interface, and no pipeline file contains an if solana branch. This chapter covers that handler and its machinery: a four-RPC state poller ticking every 400 ms, two deliberately different "highest slot" aggregates, a commitment system where "finalized" means one thing to a cache and another to a router, and a cache key that preserves base58 case on purpose.

How SVM plugs into the generic pipeline

The extension point is ArchitectureHandler (common/architecture.go:11–18): six hooks — project/network/upstream pre- and post-forward, plus NewJsonRpcErrorExtractor. A package-level map, ArchitectureRegistry (common/architecture.go:22), is populated only by init() functions of architecture packages; architecture/svm/handler.go:10–12 registers &SvmArchitectureHandler{}. Every pipeline stage (erpc/projects.go, erpc/networks.go, upstream/upstream.go) resolves the handler and calls the matching hook. Adding a chain is a handler package plus one registry entry; zero pipeline changes. The interface, verbatim:

// ArchitectureHandler abstracts all architecture-specific pipeline hooks.
// Each architecture (evm, svm, …) registers exactly one handler via its package init().
// Pipeline files dispatch through the registry — they never need to change for a new chain.
type ArchitectureHandler interface {
	HandleProjectPreForward(ctx context.Context, network Network, req *NormalizedRequest) (handled bool, resp *NormalizedResponse, err error)
	HandleNetworkPreForward(ctx context.Context, network Network, upstreams []Upstream, req *NormalizedRequest) (handled bool, resp *NormalizedResponse, err error)
	HandleNetworkPostForward(ctx context.Context, network Network, req *NormalizedRequest, resp *NormalizedResponse, err error) (*NormalizedResponse, error)
	HandleUpstreamPreForward(ctx context.Context, network Network, upstream Upstream, req *NormalizedRequest, skipCacheRead bool) (handled bool, resp *NormalizedResponse, err error)
	HandleUpstreamPostForward(ctx context.Context, network Network, upstream Upstream, req *NormalizedRequest, resp *NormalizedResponse, err error, skipCacheRead bool) (*NormalizedResponse, error)
	NewJsonRpcErrorExtractor() JsonRpcErrorExtractor
}

— common/architecture.go:8–18 (verbatim).

The handler is a thin dispatcher; real logic lives in the subpackage:

  • HandleProjectPreForward (handler.go:19–46) answers getGenesisHash from a hardcoded table, then injects the configured network commitment into request params — before the network-layer cache read. It also normalizes commitment on writes via method-specific fields (preflightCommitment for sendTransaction, commitment for simulateTransaction/requestAirdrop, hooks.go:388–404).
  • HandleNetworkPreForward (handler.go:48–60) runs the getBlock/getConfirmedBlock availability gate.
  • HandleNetworkPostForward (handler.go:62–83) corrects getSlot responses. getBlockHeight is deliberately excluded: height trails slot by every skipped slot (tens of millions on mainnet-beta), and flooring a height with a slot number would make the canonical tx-expiry check see every transaction as permanently expired.
  • HandleUpstreamPostForward (handler.go:85–112) guards non-retryable writes and harvests context.slot back into the poller.

The placement is load-bearing (handler.go:31–37): injection mutates params and invalidates the memoized CacheHash (InvalidateCacheHash, common/json_rpc.go:1433), so running it after the cache GET would key the read on pre-injection params and the write on post-injection params — a permanent cache miss for commitment-defaulted requests. The project layer is the earliest safe, upstream-agnostic place.

The SVM state poller

Each SVM upstream gets a SvmStatePoller (architecture/svm/svm_state_poller.go), bootstrapped after fail-closed genesis validation. It fires four statically-allocated payloads (:67–73) on a 400 ms ticker (DefaultPollInterval, :21–23), gated by a configurable debounce (default 400 ms, one slot). The ticker stays at the cheap fixed cadence while the gate throttles fan-out; the gate must not drive the ticker period, because it compares against lastPollAt recorded at poll completion and would skip every other tick.

The four RPCs — getHealth, getSlot{processed}, getSlot{finalized}, getMaxShredInsertSlot — are throttled asymmetrically, on purpose:

  • getHealth runs every 5th eligible poll (healthPollEveryNTicks = 5). On paid vendors the poller is the dominant background cost (measured ~3.7 calls/sec on solana-devnet pre-throttle), and its value is a near-static boolean feeding only the cordon edge. A failed probe is never throttled — an unhealthy verdict cordons the upstream, and riding out the window would multiply a 400 ms outage by N.
  • The two getSlot calls are live bounds (getSlot{finalized} is the getBlock guard's bound; getSlot{processed} bounds non-finalized routing), so they run every eligible poll unless live traffic has proven freshness. upstreamPostForward_trackContextSlot harvests context.slot from envelope responses via SuggestLatestSlot/SuggestFinalizedSlot (hooks.go:700–739); when both views are fresher than the debounce window, the two polls are skipped, bounded at 4 consecutive skips (maxConsecutiveSlotPollSkips = 4) so traffic can never starve independent verification.
  • getMaxShredInsertSlot always runs: traffic carries no equivalent signal, and a throttled watermark would go stale against the guard's staleness-margin math and start rejecting servable slots.

Accepted slots feed shared-state counters with a 1024-slot rollback tolerance (DefaultToleratedSlotRollback, :19); a deeper backward jump is the non-canonical/wrong-node signal (fork swap, snapshot restore), recorded per head axis. The counters' OnValue callbacks are the only feed into the common health tracker (SetLatestBlockNumber/SetFinalizedBlockNumber, :172–182), so score-based selection sees slots as block numbers; Solana slots carry no block timestamp, so 0 is passed.

The shred-insert watermark is the silent-stale detector: maxShredInsertSlot − processedSlot measures ingestion lag, and a node receiving shreds but not replaying them answers getHealth "ok" while reads go stale. Lag over 100 slots (MaxShredInsertSlotLagThreshold, common/architecture_svm.go:56) cordons the upstream out of selection — edge-triggered via cordonedByHealth, so it never re-stamps every 400 ms and a recovery lifts only its own cordon, never an operator's manual one. A cold poller cannot cordon: it starts healthy, and unknown is not unhealthy.

Majority vs max: two tips, on purpose

erpc/networks.go exposes four pool aggregates; conflating them is the trap.

  • SvmHighestLatestSlot / SvmHighestFinalizedSlot (networks.go:1372–1390) are majority picks via evm.PickServedTip (floor(N/2)-th highest) — what eRPC advertises to clients. A lone fast or rogue upstream must not inflate the promised head.
  • SvmHighestFinalizedSlotMax (networks.go:1409–1424) and SvmHighestIndexedSlot (networks.go:1443–1460) are pool maxima, used only by rejection gates: never reject a block the most-ahead upstream actually has. With roots at 1000/1000/1100, the majority tip reports 1000 and a majority-based guard would null out ~100 slots the third upstream holds.

Stated inline at hooks.go:504–514: advertise no more than min(finalizedMajority, indexedTip); serve up to min(finalizedMax, indexedTip). The max accessors read pollers directly because they run on every getBlock pre-forward and must not allocate per request.

The finality model: injected, classified, routed

Three predicates, kept apart deliberately.

resolveCommitment (hooks.go:265) is the single source of truth for "what commitment does eRPC pin." It reads request shape plus network config — never mutation state — so it answers identically before and after injection. A caller-supplied commitment anywhere in params wins and is never rewritten. Otherwise, if svm.commitment is configured and the method injectable, it prescribes set-or-append on the method's options index; it returns "" when nothing is pinned. The injected default is clamped (clampCommitmentForMethod, hooks.go:130–138): methods rejecting processed (getBlock, getConfirmedBlock, getBlocks, getBlocksWithLimit, getSignaturesForAddress, getTransaction — Agave answers -32602) get confirmed. Only the injected default is clamped; an explicit processed request gets the honest -32602.

effectiveCommitment (hooks.go:361–378) answers the different question "which slot does the node evaluate this at," folding in Solana's documented default, finalized, when nothing is pinned. Routing uses this — the getBlock guard, the getSlot floor, which counter the filters compare, which view a harvested context.slot belongs to. Treating "" as unknown used to forward implicit-commitment getBlock into the ~60-slot band above the finalized root that every upstream answers -32004 for — measured at 71% of devnet getBlock traffic.

GetFinality (finality.go:158–185) answers "is this response immutable enough to cache," and is the strictest:

  1. neverCacheMethods (finality.go:32–51) — writes, sub-slot transient snapshots (getLatestBlockhash, getFeeForMessage, getSignatureStatuses, getEpochInfo, …), and direct balance reads (getBalance, getTokenAccountBalance) — are Realtime; the cache hard-skips them regardless of policy.
  2. alwaysFinalizedMethods (getInflationReward, getBlockTime) — immutable by construction — are Finalized.
  3. slotPinnedMethods (getBlock, getConfirmedBlock, getTransaction) are Finalized only at commitment finalized; below that, Unfinalized, since a minority-fork switch can still drop them.
  4. Everything else is Realtime — the load-bearing rule. commitment: finalized on Solana means the state at the latest rooted slot, a head advancing every ~400 ms, not an immutability guarantee. getBalance at finalized answers a different question every slot. Classifying it Finalized would be a permanent-cache bug: DataFinalityStateFinalized is the zero value an unset-finality policy matches, and an unset TTL means no expiry.

IsFinalizedCommitment (finality.go:208–213) is the routing-side twin, following effectiveCommitment including the node default. erpc/networks.go:1920–1925 documents why the slot-lag filter gates on it rather than req.Finality(): a moving-head read at finalized commitment classifies Realtime for caching, yet the node still evaluates it against its rooted slot — the exact counter the filter compares.

"Finalized" means different things to a cache and a router. Splitting GetFinality (cacheability — strict, one-way-door conservative) from IsFinalizedCommitment (routing — follows the node's default) is the load-bearing design decision.

Cache specifics

SvmJsonRpcCache (architecture/svm/json_rpc_cache.go) reuses the shared data.CachePolicy + data.Connector abstractions; SVM and EVM can share one storage backend since network ids (svm:mainnet-beta vs evm:1) form disjoint partition-key namespaces.

The critical divergence: it never uses req.CacheHash(). The shared hasher (common/json_rpc.go hashValue) lowercases every string param — right for EVM hex, catastrophic for case-sensitive base58 pubkeys and signatures, where two distinct valid accounts differing only by case would collapse onto one entry. svmRequestKey (json_rpc_cache.go:477–498) marshals params with encoding/json (stdlib sorts map keys, so the key is deterministic) and SHA-256-hashes method || 0x00 || params with case intact:

// svmRequestKey derives the per-request cache key for SVM.
//
// It deliberately does NOT use req.CacheHash(): the shared hasher
// (common/json_rpc.go hashValue) lowercases every string param, which is the
// right normalization for EVM hex but catastrophic here — Solana base58
// pubkeys and transaction signatures are case-sensitive, so two DISTINCT valid
// accounts differing only by letter case would collapse onto one key and be
// served each other's data. This key preserves case exactly.
//
// ...
func svmRequestKey(rpcReq *common.JsonRpcRequest) (string, error) {
	if rpcReq == nil {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("cannot derive svm cache key from a nil json-rpc request")
	}
	params := rpcReq.Params
	if params == nil {
		// Normalize "no params" and "params: []" to the same key — they are the
		// same call, and json.Marshal would otherwise emit `null` vs `[]`.
		params = []interface{}{}
	}
	encoded, err := json.Marshal(params)
	if err != nil {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("failed to encode svm cache key params: %w", err)
	}
	h := sha256.New()
	// Method is hashed as well as prefixed so a method name containing the ':'
	// separator cannot forge another method's key.
	_, _ = h.Write([]byte(rpcReq.Method))
	_, _ = h.Write([]byte{0})
	_, _ = h.Write(encoded)
	return fmt.Sprintf("%s:%x", rpcReq.Method, h.Sum(nil)), nil
}

— architecture/svm/json_rpc_cache.go:456–498 (verbatim, trimmed).

The partition (group) key is <networkId>:<slotRef> (:443–454, 554–577), where slotRef is the request's minContextSlot or *. Since slotRef derives from the params, a (method, params) tuple always yields the same group key on Get and Set, so doGet always reads ConnectorMainIndex. There is no block-timestamp age guard (EVM's ttl_rejected miss branch has no SVM counterpart): only genuinely immutable responses classify Finalized, so the realtime policy's TTL bounds staleness.

RequestKey (:508–517) exposes the same identity to the pipeline. Any "are these two requests the same?" decision on SVM — cache, in-flight multiplexing — must use it, never CacheHash(). Payloads are zstd-compressed above a 512-byte threshold at SpeedFastest (Solana getBlock responses routinely exceed 1 MB); decompression keys off the zstd magic number, not current config. Writes are async like EVM; JSON-RPC error bodies are never stored.

Slot lag and context-slot filtering

Two SVM-only selection prefilters run in erpc/networks.go:1907–1966:

  • FilterByFinalizedSlotLag (slot_lag.go:32–54) drops upstreams whose finalized slot trails the reference by more than maxFinalizedSlotLag (default 100) — only when a consensus policy is active and IsFinalizedCommitment is true. The reference is not the raw pool max: ReferenceFinalizedSlot (slot_lag.go:107–133) clamps to the runner-up when the leader outruns it by more than maxLag, so one liar cannot shrink the pool to itself. Upstreams without pollers, with zero slots, or non-SVM types always pass.
  • FilterByMinContextSlot (slot_lag.go:142–157) excludes upstreams behind the caller's minContextSlot at the request's commitment — forwarding there is a guaranteed -32016. Finalized-commitment requests compare against each upstream's finalized slot, weaker commitments against the processed tip.

Both fail open: if filtering would empty the pool, the original list is returned — stale data beats a deadlocked consensus, and the -32016 failover path still reports the truth when every upstream trails.

Upstream sweep and write handling

IsNonRetryableWriteMethod (architecture/svm/util.go:20–28) covers sendTransaction, sendRawTransaction, requestAirdrop. Solana broadcasts are same-signature idempotent on-chain, so retrying sendTransaction risks not double-spend but duplicate broadcasts burning vendor quota; requestAirdrop mints per call — a failover after an effective first attempt mints twice. simulateTransaction is absent: read-only, safe to retry.

IsSingleDispatchWriteMethod (util.go:46–48) is the strict subset — only requestAirdrop — that must reach at most one upstream per client call: consensus treats same-signature fan-out as one transaction, but an N-participant airdrop vote mints N times and disputes the N signatures. It lives in svm/ because erpc/ deliberately does not import consensus/ (dependency cycle).

Post-forward (hooks.go:758–771), write errors are wrapped ClientSideException with retryableTowardNetwork(false) — the network loop bails specifically on that code. The wrap applies only to attempts that may have reached the wire. preDispatchErrorCodes (hooks.go:782–790) — selection rejection, local rate limit, open breaker — prove the request was never transmitted, so the sweep stays free to fail over; transport errors, timeouts, and 5xx are excluded, since "the server failed" is not permission to re-run a mint.

Error normalization

JsonRpcErrorExtractor (architecture/svm/error_normalizer.go) maps Agave's RpcCustomError codes (-32001..-32019, name-aligned 1:1 with the validator source) onto eRPC's StandardError taxonomy, under two invariants.

First, the wire code is a faithful passthrough: Solana clients dispatch on the exact number (@solana/kit maps -32002/-32005/-32016 to named classes) and read error.data alongside; eRPC's routing verdict lives in the outer error class only. This creates the documented collision: eRPC's own constants reuse -32005 for CapacityExceeded and -32016 for Unauthorized, which Agave assigns to NodeUnhealthy and MinContextSlotNotReached. The invariant keeping them apart: on an SVM path eRPC never synthesizes either number, so -32005/-32016 in an SVM body always came from the upstream and mean the Agave semantic. eRPC's own capacity verdicts go out as HTTP 429 with -32000; unauthorized uses -32600.

Second, the skipped-slot codes are swept but never waited on. -32007 (SlotSkipped — "skipped OR missing due to ledger jump") and -32009 (LongTermStorageSlotSkipped — "skipped, OR missing in long-term storage", where the "or" is per-provider archive policy) map to MissingData marked permanent (newSweptSkipMissingData, error_normalizer.go:438–447): retryable across upstreams for one full sweep — a ledger jump is node-local, archive completeness per-provider — but once every provider returns them, no time-delayed re-sweep runs, because waiting cannot un-skip a slot or backfill someone else's archive. Codeless vendor variants ("missing in long-term storage", "ledger jump" in the -32000 bucket) get the same treatment by message match. The extractor also carries the upstream's data member verbatim — -32002 packs an RpcSimulateTransactionResult whose logs @solana/web3.js requires — and classifies HTTP 401/403 as auth failures regardless of any JSON-RPC body present.

BDS / gRPC connector

The gRPC/BDS connector participates only as a cache connector (driver: grpc, data/grpc.go:58–72), allowlisting exactly one SVM method, getBlock, in json/jsonParsed encodings. Because Agave reports skipped slots as JSON-RPC errors, the BDS reader cannot serve them and they fall through to live upstreams (clients/grpc_bds_client.go:1525–1534, TODO BDA-3110). networkId is required in connector config since eth_chainId is unimplemented on BDS readers. SVM upstreams themselves are HTTP-only; other schemes error at client registration (clients/registry.go:122–142), and WebSocket is unimplemented everywhere.

Genesis validation at bootstrap is fail-closed against knownSvmGenesisHashes (common/architecture_svm.go:81–87: mainnet-beta, devnet, testnet under solana); unknown clusters run only with checkGenesisHash: true (upstream/upstream.go:354–368). There is no SVM-specific failsafe struct — SVM networks use the same failsafe config shape as EVM.

Edge cases and gotchas

  1. Commitment injection at the project layer invalidates the memoized CacheHash so read and write key identically; injecting later would permanently miss for commitment-defaulted requests.
  2. Only the injected default is clamped (processed → confirmed). A caller explicitly asking for processed on getBlock gets the honest -32602 — never silently upgraded.
  3. The getBlock guard fails open when the indexed frontier is unknown: a cold poller or a vendor without getMaxShredInsertSlot must not cost requests every upstream could serve.
  4. getSlot at commitment confirmed is never corrected — no confirmed tip is tracked, and flooring with the processed tip would return an unconfirmed slot.
  5. The guard's staleness margin is 2 + debounce/400ms (3 at defaults, 7 at a 2 s debounce): pool tips are snapshots refreshed at most once per debounce while the chain advances a slot per ~400 ms; without the margin, callers freshly reading getSlot(confirmed) were short-circuited ~30 times/min.
  6. Both selection prefilters fail open — stale data beats a deadlocked consensus.
  7. Non-retryable-write protection yields for pre-dispatch failures (selection rejection, rate limit, open breaker): a write that never reached the wire can safely fail over; one that may have landed must not be re-broadcast.
  8. Any request-identity decision on SVM must use svm.RequestKey, never req.CacheHash() — the shared hasher lowercases params and would collapse case-distinct base58 pubkeys.
  9. getGenesisHash is answered from the hardcoded table with zero upstream calls; unknown clusters are never fabricated.

14. Configuration reference

A complete reference for every configuration block in an eRPC (erpc.yaml or erpc.ts) config file, with types, defaults, and what each option actually does. Grounded in the config schema in common/config.go, defaults in common/defaults.go, and the config docs under docs/pages/config/. Defaults below were cross-checked against those sources; anything not directly verifiable is marked (verify).

Conventions

  • Duration fields accept Go duration strings ("30s", "500ms", "10m"). A bare integer is interpreted as milliseconds — maxTimeout: 150 means 150 ms, not 150 s. This is the single most common misconfiguration.
  • Wildcard patterns (used by method, network, ignoreMethods, allowedOrigins, matchDomain, use-upstream, forwardHeaders, etc.) use eRPC's boolean/glob grammar: * (any sequence), ? (one char), . (any single char — note: a literal dot is NOT required to match a dot), | (OR), & (AND), ! (NOT), parentheses. Values starting 0x support numeric comparison prefixes (>=, <=, >, <, =). No escape syntax.
  • URL routing: requests are POST /<projectId>/<architecture>/<chainId> (e.g. /main/evm/1), or /<projectId>/<alias> such as /main/arbitrum. Network aliases work in URL paths only, not in the body's networkId field. Any non-POST/non-OPTIONS request is treated as a healthcheck.
  • Config file formats: YAML or TypeScript (createConfig from @erpc-cloud/config). All YAML keys shown here map 1:1 to TS object keys.

Timeouts and encoding

FieldTypeDefaultWhat it does
server.maxTimeoutDuration150sRequired non-zero. Hard per-HTTP-request deadline covering the whole lifecycle (retries + hedges included). POST timeout → HTTP 200 + JSON-RPC -32603; other methods → 504. Must exceed your largest network failsafe.timeout.
server.readTimeoutDuration30shttp.Server.ReadTimeout (headers + body).
server.writeTimeoutDuration120shttp.Server.WriteTimeout; only matters at final flush since responses are buffered.
server.enableGzipbooltrueResponse compression (first write decides; chunks < 1024 bytes are not compressed). Inbound gzip bodies are always accepted regardless of this flag.

There is no request-body size limit and no batch-size limit; effective limits are readTimeout and process memory. Hardcoded constants: IdleTimeout 300s, MaxHeaderBytes 1 MiB, shutdown budget 30s, TLS 1.2 min.
